newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin prepares for summit with Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin prepares for summit with Clinton.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin took a timeout on Tuesday after launching Russia's biggest government reshuffle in five years and prepared for a summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki on Tursday and Friday.
Presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had gone to the Gorky-9 residence outside Moscow and his only planned meeting was with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.

Primakov briefed him on three days of pre-summit talks in Washington which left Russia and the United States divided on NATO's eastward expansion plans, although he signalled that Moscow wanted an accommodation with Washington.

Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin's foreign policy advisor, Dmitry Ryurikov, as saying the Kremlin hoped there was still a chance that NATO could reconsider its expansion plans if not for political reasons then for their huge cost.
Ryurikov said joining NATO will put great financial strains both on the new Eastern European members and on the alliance itself.
"We hope that in the next few months everyone, including NATO, will weigh agains all financial consequences of the alliances possible expansion to the east," he said.
He said Russia was ready to offer any security guarantees to Eastern Europe individually or together with NATO.

Yeltsin, 66, has taken a tough stance before the summit, ruling out concessions and criticising U.S. policy towards Russia. But he has also made clear he is determined to prevent a return to Cold War tensions.
The summit will be Yeltsin's first foreign trip since last April and offers him a chance to prove himself on the world stage after heart surgery on November 5.
He has already reasserted his authority after returning to the Kremlin last month following long absences caused by the heart problems and then pneumonia.
A government reshuffle launched on Monday reinforced the cabinet with senior reformist-minded members.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin is now backed by two first deputies -- Yeltsin's former chief of staff Anatoly Chubais, 41, who had spearheaded Russia's privatisation campaign, and Boris Nemtsov, 37, former reformist mayor of Nizhny Novgorod region.

"The main task of the government will be broadening and speeding up the reforms in the social and economic spheres, the practical side being the top priority," said Chernomyrdin, presenting Chubais to the ministry's officials.
"The situation in the country has to be quickly changed to the better and all conditions for it have been created."
Some conservative ministers lost their jobs or were demoted, although the full line-up has not been revealed.
Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov stayed as a deputy prime minister. Some questions lingered over Defence Minister Igor Rodionov's future but Primakov looked set to remain.
Chubais also took the Finance Ministry portfolio in the most far-reaching cabinet changes since liberal Yegor Gaidar became post-Soviet Russia's first de-facto premier in 1991.
Chubais told commercial NTV television that Yeltsin's decree reshaping the government and scrapping some ministries was not the last step in the cabinet changes.
